drills.q: A DAG file has `config = Variable.get('my_config')` at module scope, outside any task. What's wrong with this, concretely?
drills.a: The scheduler's DAG File Processor re-parses the file on every scan interval (a few seconds), so this line — and the DB hit it makes — executes on every single parse, not once at authoring time. Move it inside a task callable so it only runs at task execution time.

drills.q: A DAG is scheduled `@daily` starting 2026-01-01. For the run whose logical_date is 2026-08-01, when does it actually execute, and why?
drills.a: Shortly after midnight on 2026-08-02. The scheduler can't guarantee it has complete data for the interval [2026-08-01, 2026-08-02) until that period has fully elapsed, so it waits until the interval ends before starting the run.

drills.q: A task uses `context['ds']` to compute 'data through today' for a filter condition. What's the bug, and what should it use instead?
drills.a: `ds`/logical_date is the START of the data interval, not the end — using it as 'through today' silently shifts the filter window back by one interval. It should use `data_interval_end` for 'data through the end of this period'.

drills.q: 50 DAGs each run an S3KeySensor in default poke mode, waiting up to 6 hours for files to land, against a worker pool sized for 20 concurrent slots. Diagnose the cluster-wide symptom and fix it.
drills.a: Worker-slot starvation: each poke-mode sensor blocks a worker for its entire wait, so with 50 long waits against 20 slots, unrelated tasks across the whole cluster queue and run late with no crash anywhere. Fix: set deferrable=True on the sensors so they hand the wait to the triggerer and release the worker slot entirely.

drills.q: A task returns a full pandas DataFrame from a `@task`-decorated function and a downstream task consumes it as an argument. Why is this a design smell, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Return values are passed via XCom, whose default backend stores values in the metadata database — sized for small control values, not bulk data; it degrades DB/UI performance for the whole instance. Fix: write the DataFrame to durable storage (e.g. S3 parquet) and return just the path/URI through XCom.

drills.q: 20 independent DAGs each cap their own concurrency at max_active_tasks=5, but they all query the same downstream Postgres replica, which starts refusing connections during peak hours. Why didn't max_active_tasks prevent this, and what fixes it?
drills.a: max_active_tasks caps concurrency within a single DAG only — it has no visibility into other DAGs, so 20 DAGs at 5 each can still open 100 concurrent connections to the same resource. Fix: create a named pool sized below the replica's safe connection limit and assign every task touching that resource to it, capping concurrency across all DAGs collectively.

drills.q: Your team relies on Airflow's SLA feature to page on-call when a DAG misses its freshness target. After upgrading to Airflow 3.0, SLA-based DAGs stop working. What replaced it, and what's the actual behavioral improvement, not just the API change?
drills.a: Deadline Alerts (3.1+) replaced SLAs (removed in 3.0). The old SLA mechanism only evaluated whether a deadline was missed after the DAG run finished — late detection if the DAG ran long. Deadline Alerts evaluate at the calculated deadline itself and fire within roughly one scheduler heartbeat, materially faster for on-call paging.

drills.q: A mapped task (`.expand()`) fed by an upstream task that returns a list from an unvalidated API response explodes to 40,000 task instances overnight, and the scheduler becomes unresponsive. What guard should have prevented this, and what else besides scheduler CPU gets hurt?
drills.a: max_map_length (default 1024) should cap the expansion, plus validating/capping the upstream list size before mapping. Besides scheduler CPU, the metadata database takes damage too — every mapped instance is rows in task_instance tables, so a runaway expand() degrades DB write throughput for every other DAG sharing that database, not just the offending one.

drills.q: Explain what changed about worker-to-metadata-database access in Airflow 3.0 and name one real migration pain point it causes for teams upgrading from 2.x.
drills.a: Workers no longer connect to the metadata DB directly; all state transitions, XCom, heartbeats, and connection/variable fetching go through a new Task Execution API (REST layer), improving security and enabling non-Python runtimes. Migration pain point: custom operators that previously queried the metadata DB directly via raw SQLAlchemy (e.g., checking another DAG's state) break entirely and must be rewritten against the supported API or mechanisms like ExternalTaskSensor.

drills.q: What are Airflow Assets (formerly Datasets) and how do they reduce reliance on ExternalTaskSensor-style cross-DAG polling?
drills.a: An Asset represents a logical piece of data a task declares it produces. Downstream DAGs can be scheduled to trigger the instant an upstream task updates an Asset they depend on — push-based and data-centric — instead of a sensor polling another DAG's task state, which still occupies a worker or triggerer slot doing the polling.

drills.q: Design pools and priority for a cluster running one deadline-critical nightly warehouse rebuild alongside 40 small hourly DAGs, all hitting the same Postgres read replica.
drills.a: Put every task touching that replica (from any DAG) into one named pool sized below the replica's safe connection limit. Give the nightly rebuild's tasks a higher priority_weight so it wins scheduling contention for that pool near its deadline. Set max_active_runs=1 on the rebuild DAG to prevent an accidental overlapping run from doubling load on the same resource.
